category.name: Privacy & compliance breach
category.description: Regulatory and privacy obligations after an incident: breach notification decisions, regulator inquiries, legal hold, insurance and third-party notices.

playbooks.name: GDPR 72-hour supervisory authority notification decision
playbooks.summary: Use when a security incident may involve EU or UK personal data and the controller must decide within 72 hours of awareness whether to notify the supervisory authority and data subjects.

preparation: Name the DPO and lead supervisory authority for each EU establishment in the IR contact list
Keep a GDPR Article 33 notification template with the required fields pre-filled
Maintain a record of processing activities that maps systems to personal data categories
identification: Record the exact time the organization became aware of the breach, since the 72-hour clock starts there
Identify categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and records involved
Determine whether the incident affects confidentiality, integrity or availability of personal data
Assess likely consequences for individuals such as identity theft, discrimination or financial loss
Check whether the data was encrypted with keys that were not compromised
containment: Convene DPO, Legal and IR lead to agree a risk rating and notification decision
Document the reasoning if the decision is that notification is not required
Submit the Article 33 notification to the lead authority within 72 hours, with phased updates if facts are incomplete
eradication: Assess whether high risk to individuals requires direct Article 34 communication to data subjects
Draft data subject notices in clear language with recommended protective steps
Coordinate with processors that hold the affected data for their facts and actions
recovery: Send supplementary information to the authority as the investigation progresses
Answer authority questions through the DPO with a single source of truth
Record the breach in the internal breach register regardless of notification
lessons: Measure time from awareness to notification decision
Review whether awareness was delayed by slow escalation from the SOC to the DPO
Update the processing record where systems lacked data mapping

splunk.title: Earliest detection event for the awareness timeline
splunk.spl: index=notable search_name="*" (dest="<affected_host>" OR user="<affected_user>") | stats earliest(_time) as first_alert values(search_name) as rules values(owner) as owner by dest | convert ctime(first_alert)

splunk.title: Record counts accessed in affected EU systems
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype IN ("mssql:audit","mysql:audit") database_name IN ("<eu_db>") earliest=<incident_start> | stats sum(affected_rows) as rows dc(object_name) as tables by server_principal_name client_ip

playbooks.name: HIPAA breach risk assessment for a PHI incident
playbooks.summary: Use when an incident involves protected health information and the covered entity or business associate must run the four-factor risk assessment and decide on notification within 60 days.

preparation: Keep a HIPAA four-factor breach risk assessment form approved by the Privacy Officer
List business associate agreements with their breach notification terms
Know the HHS OCR breach portal submission process and who holds the account
identification: Determine the nature and extent of PHI involved, including identifiers and likelihood of re-identification
Identify the unauthorized person who used or received the PHI
Establish whether the PHI was actually acquired or viewed, using access logs and forensics
Record the extent to which risk has been mitigated, such as recipient deletion attestations
Note the discovery date, which starts the 60-day individual notification limit
containment: Have the Privacy Officer conclude whether there is a low probability of compromise
Document the full assessment in the HIPAA incident log whether or not it is a reportable breach
Check whether an exception applies, such as unintentional workforce access in good faith
eradication: Draft individual notification letters with the required content and toll-free contact if needed
Prepare media notice and HHS notice if 500 or more residents of a state or jurisdiction are affected
Notify the covered entity promptly if the organization is acting as a business associate
recovery: Mail individual notices without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days from discovery
Submit the HHS breach report on the appropriate schedule for the breach size
Track returned mail and provide substitute notice where contact details are outdated
lessons: Review the security rule safeguards that failed and update the risk analysis
Measure time from discovery to completed risk assessment
Train the workforce on the specific behavior that caused the incident

splunk.title: PHI record access by unauthorized party
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="ehr:audit" user="<unauthorized_user>" earliest=<incident_start> | stats dc(patient_id) as patients count values(action) as actions by user workstation

splunk.title: Exports and prints of PHI in the window
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="ehr:audit" action IN ("export","print","download") earliest=<incident_start> latest=<incident_end> | stats dc(patient_id) as patients by user action

playbooks.name: PCI DSS cardholder data compromise
playbooks.summary: Use when payment card data may have been stolen from a POS, e-commerce checkout or cardholder data environment, triggering acquirer and card brand obligations and possibly a PFI investigation.

preparation: Keep the acquiring bank and payment processor incident contacts with contract requirements
Maintain a current cardholder data environment network diagram and asset list
Identify a PCI Forensic Investigator firm in advance
identification: Determine the compromise vector: POS memory scraper, web skimmer on checkout or database theft
Identify the window of exposure from the first malicious change to containment
Estimate the number of PANs processed in the exposure window by brand
Check whether CVV, track data or PIN blocks could have been captured
Preserve CDE system images and logs before remediation for the PFI
containment: Notify the acquirer within the timeframe required by the merchant agreement
Isolate compromised POS terminals or remove the malicious script from checkout pages
Do not wipe or rebuild CDE systems until the PFI agrees evidence is preserved
eradication: Remove the malware or skimmer and close the initial access path
Rotate CDE administrative credentials and payment gateway API keys
Apply integrity monitoring to checkout scripts and POS binaries
recovery: Provide the PFI report and remediation evidence to the acquirer and brands
Supply at-risk account lists to the acquirer through the approved secure channel
Assess whether state breach notification to cardholders also applies
lessons: Implement client-side script monitoring for payment pages
Review CDE segmentation that failed to limit the compromise
Track fines, assessments and remediation costs for the board

splunk.title: Changes to checkout page scripts
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.object="*checkout*" OR All_Changes.object="*payment*.js" by All_Changes.user All_Changes.dest All_Changes.object _time span=1h

splunk.title: Outbound connections from CDE hosts to unknown destinations
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_zone="cde" All_Traffic.dest_zone="untrust" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port | lookup approved_cde_egress.csv dest as All_Traffic.dest OUTPUT approved | where isnull(approved)

splunk.title: Transaction volume in exposure window
splunk.spl: index=payments sourcetype="payment:gateway" earliest=<exposure_start> latest=<exposure_end> | stats dc(card_token) as cards count by card_brand

playbooks.name: US state data breach notification analysis
playbooks.summary: Use when personal information of US residents was or may have been acquired and you must determine which state laws apply, who to notify and what content and timing each requires.

preparation: Retain outside privacy counsel with a current state-by-state breach law matrix
Keep a notification vendor on contract for mailing, call center and credit monitoring
Ensure customer and employee records store state of residence
identification: Confirm whether the exposed data elements meet state definitions of personal information
Determine whether data was encrypted and whether the key was also compromised
Count affected individuals by state of residence from the dataset
Identify states with attorney general or regulator notice requirements triggered by the counts
Confirm whether law enforcement has requested a delay in notification
containment: Have counsel confirm the list of applicable states and each deadline
Decide on credit monitoring or identity protection offers, noting states that require them
Prepare regulator notices for states requiring attorney general filing
eradication: Draft consumer notice letters meeting each state's content requirements
Validate mailing addresses and remove duplicates through the notification vendor
Set up the call center with an approved FAQ script
recovery: Mail notices and submit regulator filings, recording dates sent per state
Notify consumer reporting agencies if the count exceeds thresholds in applicable states
Track inbound inquiries and complaints from the call center
lessons: Reduce collection or retention of the data elements that triggered notification
Measure how long data mapping by state took and improve it
Record total cost per notified individual for insurance and budgeting

splunk.title: Affected records by state from the exposed dataset index
splunk.spl: index=ir_scoping sourcetype="csv" source="*<exposed_dataset>*" | stats dc(customer_id) as individuals by state | sort - individuals

splunk.title: Data elements present in exposed records
splunk.spl: index=ir_scoping source="*<exposed_dataset>*" | eval has_ssn=if(isnotnull(ssn) AND ssn!="",1,0), has_dl=if(isnotnull(drivers_license) AND drivers_license!="",1,0), has_acct=if(isnotnull(account_number) AND account_number!="",1,0) | stats sum(has_ssn) as ssn sum(has_dl) as dl sum(has_acct) as acct by state

playbooks.name: SEC Form 8-K materiality determination for a cyber incident
playbooks.summary: Use when a US-listed company has a significant cyber incident and must determine materiality, then file Item 1.05 of Form 8-K within four business days of a materiality determination.

preparation: Define a disclosure committee with the CFO, General Counsel, CISO and IR lead
Document materiality criteria with quantitative and qualitative factors in advance
Keep securities counsel and the filing agent on call
identification: Brief the disclosure committee with known facts: systems affected, data impacted, operational disruption
Estimate financial impact: revenue loss, remediation cost, ransom, legal exposure and customer churn
Assess qualitative factors such as reputational harm, regulatory scrutiny and customer relationships
Record the date and rationale of the materiality determination, which starts the four-business-day clock
Check whether the Attorney General national security delay could apply, through counsel
containment: Draft Item 1.05 disclosure describing nature, scope, timing and material impact without operational detail
Review the draft with counsel to avoid disclosing information that would hinder remediation
Restrict insider trading by placing relevant insiders under a blackout
eradication: File the 8-K within four business days of the materiality determination
Coordinate customer, employee and press communications to match the filing
Brief the board audit committee on the filing and next steps
recovery: File an 8-K amendment when previously unavailable material information becomes known
Align 10-K Item 1C risk management disclosures with lessons from the incident
Keep the disclosure committee minutes and evidence with the incident record
lessons: Measure time from incident detection to materiality determination
Review whether escalation criteria from IR to the disclosure committee worked
Update the materiality framework based on this incident's facts

splunk.title: Scope of affected hosts for disclosure briefing
splunk.spl: index=notable earliest=<incident_start> (search_name="*Ransomware*" OR search_name="*Exfil*" OR urgency IN ("critical","high")) | stats dc(dest) as hosts dc(user) as users values(search_name) as detections by orig_sourcetype

splunk.title: Business service outage timeline
splunk.spl: index=itsi_summary OR index=* sourcetype="nagios:*" (service="<critical_service>" OR host="<critical_host>") earliest=<incident_start> | timechart span=1h count(eval(status="CRITICAL")) as critical

playbooks.name: NIS2 or DORA significant incident reporting
playbooks.summary: Use when an EU essential or important entity (NIS2) or financial entity (DORA) has an incident that may be significant or major and must be classified and reported to the CSIRT or competent authority in stages.

preparation: Confirm whether each EU entity falls under NIS2, DORA or both and record its competent authority
Adopt the classification criteria for significant (NIS2) and major (DORA) incidents in the IR runbook
Prepare report templates for the initial, intermediate and final stages
identification: Classify the incident against criteria: clients affected, duration, geographic spread, data loss, economic impact
Record awareness and classification timestamps that start the reporting clocks
Identify critical or important functions and ICT third-party providers affected
Determine whether the incident has cross-border impact on other member states
Check whether the incident also triggers GDPR breach notification
containment: Submit the NIS2 early warning within 24 hours of awareness where the incident is significant
Submit the DORA initial notification within the timelines in the regulatory technical standards
Inform recipients of the service where required about measures they can take
eradication: Send the intermediate or incident notification with updated assessment, severity and indicators
Coordinate with ICT third-party providers for their root-cause data
Share indicators with the national CSIRT where helpful
recovery: Prepare the final report with root cause, mitigation measures and cross-border impact
Answer follow-up requests from the competent authority through the compliance lead
Record reporting submissions and acknowledgements in the incident file
lessons: Review whether classification was timely and accurate against the criteria
Update the ICT third-party register and contracts if a provider caused the incident
Report lessons to the management body, which holds accountability under both regimes

splunk.title: Affected critical service availability timeline
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest="<critical_service>" by Web.status _time span=15m | eval failed=if(match('Web.status',"^5"),count,0) | stats sum(failed) as failed sum(count) as total by _time | eval error_rate=round(failed/total*100,1)

splunk.title: Distinct client accounts affected by failed sessions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="app:transactions" service="<critical_service>" status=failed earliest=<incident_start> | stats dc(client_id) as clients sum(amount) as value_affected by country

playbooks.name: Data subject access request reveals a breach
playbooks.summary: Use when fulfilling a DSAR or consumer privacy request uncovers that the person's data was exposed, misused or held in unexpected places, turning a routine request into an incident.

preparation: Give the privacy request team an escalation path to IR when they find unexpected data
Maintain a data inventory so DSAR searches cover all systems
Track DSAR response deadlines in the privacy request tool
identification: Document what the DSAR search found: unexpected systems, unauthorized sharing or evidence of exposure
Determine whether the issue affects only the requester or a wider set of individuals
Identify the system owner and how the data came to be there
Check access logs for the unexpected location to see who viewed the data
Assess whether the finding is a personal data breach requiring notification
containment: Restrict access to the unexpected data location
Separate the incident handling from the DSAR response so the deadline is still met
Preserve evidence before any cleanup changes the data
eradication: Delete data held without a lawful basis once Legal confirms
Fix the integration or export job that copied data to the wrong place
Run the same search for other individuals to scope the problem
recovery: Respond to the DSAR completely, including disclosure of recipients where required
Notify the authority and affected individuals if the breach assessment requires
Update the data inventory with the newly found data store
lessons: Add the discovered data store to regular privacy scans
Measure how often DSAR work uncovers unmapped data
Review retention rules that should have removed the data

splunk.title: Who accessed the unexpected data location
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("FileAccessed","FileDownloaded","FileModified") ObjectId="*<unexpected_location>*" | stats count earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by UserId Operation | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

splunk.title: Search other indexes for the data subject identifier
splunk.spl: index=* earliest=-90d "<subject_email>" NOT index=ir_scoping | stats count by index sourcetype source

playbooks.name: Exposure of children's personal data
playbooks.summary: Use when personal data of minors is exposed, for example from a school platform, gaming account, youth program or pediatric records, where heightened legal duties and parental notification apply.

preparation: Identify every system that stores data on children and its age thresholds
Have counsel map obligations under COPPA, GDPR-K, age-appropriate design codes and education privacy laws
Prepare parent and guardian notification templates written in plain language
identification: Confirm the ages of affected individuals from the dataset to determine which rules apply
Identify data types exposed: names, school, location, photos, chat messages, health or special needs
Assess safeguarding risks such as location data or contact details reachable by predators
Determine whether the data was accessed or downloaded by unauthorized parties
Check whether a school district or other controller owns the data and must lead notification
containment: Remove public access or disable the exposed feature immediately
Engage safeguarding leads if there is any risk of contact with children
Notify the controlling school or organization if acting as a processor
eradication: Delete data collected beyond what parental consent covered
Fix the access control or misconfiguration that exposed the records
Review third-party SDKs or analytics that received children's data
recovery: Notify parents and guardians with clear guidance on protective steps
Make regulator notifications on the timelines advised by counsel
Provide a dedicated support line for parents
lessons: Apply data minimization to children's data in the affected product
Add an age-flag to datasets so exposures can be scoped faster
Review vendor contracts for child data protections

splunk.title: Access to the exposed children's records endpoint
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count dc(Web.src) as sources sum(Web.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*<exposed_endpoint>*" Web.status=200 by Web.src Web.http_user_agent | sort - bytes

splunk.title: Third-party SDK traffic from the youth app
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.src_category="<youth_app_backend>" by Web.dest | lookup approved_processors.csv dest as Web.dest OUTPUT approved | where isnull(approved)

playbooks.name: Biometric data exposure (fingerprints, face templates, voiceprints)
playbooks.summary: Use when biometric identifiers or templates from time clocks, access control, identity verification or voice systems are exposed, which cannot be reset like passwords and carry specific legal duties.

preparation: Inventory systems that capture or store biometric templates and their vendors
Keep records of biometric consent and retention schedules where laws like Illinois BIPA apply
Confirm whether vendors store raw images or irreversible templates
identification: Determine whether raw biometric images, templates or both were exposed
Assess whether the templates are vendor-proprietary and usable outside the system
Identify the individuals affected and their states or countries of residence
Check whether consent records exist for every affected individual
Identify whether the exposure occurred at the company or at the biometric vendor
containment: Disconnect the exposed biometric database or API from external access
Suspend enrollment of new biometrics until the cause is fixed
Require the vendor to preserve logs and provide their incident report
eradication: Delete biometric data past its retention period or lacking consent
Re-enroll users with new templates if the vendor supports template revocation
Offer alternative authentication such as badges or PINs to affected staff
recovery: Notify individuals and regulators as counsel advises, noting biometric-specific laws
Update consent forms and the public retention policy
Confirm the vendor's fix through an independent test
lessons: Decide whether biometrics are necessary for the use case
Require template encryption and on-device matching in vendor selection
Review litigation exposure and insurance coverage for biometric claims

splunk.title: Access to biometric database from external sources
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest="<biometric_db>" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_port | where NOT cidrmatch("10.0.0.0/8", 'All_Traffic.src')

splunk.title: Biometric API template export calls
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="biometric:api" (endpoint="*/templates*" OR endpoint="*/export*") http_method=GET | stats count dc(subject_id) as subjects by client_id src_ip

playbooks.name: Inquiry received from a data protection or security regulator
playbooks.summary: Use when a regulator (data protection authority, FTC, state AG, sector regulator) sends a letter or request for information about a security incident or privacy practice.

preparation: Route all regulator correspondence to Legal and the privacy lead through a single intake address
Keep incident records, risk assessments and policies organized for production on request
Retain regulatory defense counsel familiar with the relevant regulator
identification: Log the request, the regulator, reference number, questions asked and the response deadline
Determine which incident or practice the inquiry concerns and whether it is already known internally
Identify the custodians and systems holding responsive information
Check whether the inquiry stems from a complaint, media report or prior notification
containment: Issue a legal hold to custodians and systems relevant to the inquiry
Appoint a single point of contact for all communication with the regulator
Request a deadline extension through counsel if the scope requires it
eradication: Gather incident timelines, logs, notifications sent and remediation evidence
Verify every factual statement in the draft response against source evidence
Remediate any outstanding gaps the inquiry highlights before responding where possible
recovery: Submit the response through counsel and confirm receipt
Track follow-up questions and commitments made to the regulator
Brief executives and the board on exposure and next steps
lessons: Review whether internal records made the response easy or slow to assemble
Close commitments made to the regulator on schedule
Update policies the inquiry showed were outdated or not followed

splunk.title: Export incident timeline evidence for the response
splunk.spl: index=notable earliest=<incident_start> latest=<incident_end> (dest="<affected_host>" OR user="<affected_user>") | table _time search_name dest user status owner comment | sort _time

splunk.title: Proof of logging coverage on affected systems
splunk.spl: | tstats count where index=* host IN ("<affected_host1>","<affected_host2>") earliest=<incident_start> by host sourcetype _time span=1d

playbooks.name: Cyber insurance notice and claim process
playbooks.summary: Use when an incident may be covered by a cyber insurance policy and you need to give timely notice, use panel vendors, track costs and avoid actions that jeopardize coverage.

preparation: Keep the policy number, insurer claims hotline and notice requirements in the IR contact sheet
List the insurer's panel breach coaches, forensics firms and negotiators
Note policy conditions such as consent before ransom payment or vendor engagement
identification: Confirm the incident type falls within insuring agreements: breach response, business interruption, extortion
Record the date the incident was discovered for notice timing under the policy
Identify retention or deductible amounts and sublimits relevant to the incident
containment: Give notice to the insurer via the claims hotline or portal as early as the policy requires
Engage panel vendors through the breach coach, or get written consent for non-panel vendors
Get insurer consent before committing to any ransom or extortion payment
eradication: Track every incident-related cost with invoices, labor hours and vendor statements
Quantify business interruption loss with Finance using the policy's calculation method
Keep privileged forensic reports under counsel direction
recovery: Submit the proof of loss with supporting documents by the policy deadline
Respond to insurer adjuster questions through counsel
Reconcile reimbursements against costs and document disputes
lessons: Review whether sublimits and retention were adequate for this incident
Update the renewal application with controls added after the incident
Record time from discovery to insurer notice

splunk.title: Downtime duration for business interruption claim
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.dest="<revenue_service>" earliest=<incident_start> by _time span=1h | eval up=if(count>0,1,0) | stats sum(eval(1-up)) as hours_down count as hours_observed

splunk.title: Hosts reimaged or restored during recovery
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false dc(All_Changes.dest) as hosts values(All_Changes.dest) as dests from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.command IN ("*reimage*","*restore*","*rebuild*") earliest=<incident_start> by All_Changes.user

playbooks.name: Legal hold and evidence preservation for an incident
playbooks.summary: Use when litigation, regulatory action or law enforcement involvement is reasonably anticipated after an incident and logs, images, mailboxes and records must be preserved defensibly.

preparation: Document the process for issuing and releasing legal holds with Legal
Ensure the SIEM, EDR and cloud log retention can be extended on demand
Keep forensic imaging tools, write blockers and evidence storage ready
identification: Identify custodians, systems, log sources and time ranges relevant to the incident
Check retention settings that would delete relevant data soon, such as 30-day EDR or 90-day log rollover
List physical evidence such as laptops, USB drives and printed documents
Confirm with Legal the scope and date of anticipated litigation
containment: Issue legal hold notices to custodians and IT system owners and track acknowledgements
Place mailboxes and OneDrive accounts on eDiscovery hold
Suspend automated deletion and retention jobs on relevant systems
eradication: Take forensic images of key hosts with hashes recorded
Export relevant SIEM and cloud logs to write-once storage
Record chain of custody for each evidence item
recovery: Confirm remediation activities like reimaging only happen after images are captured
Review hold compliance periodically and remind custodians
Release holds only on written instruction from Legal
lessons: Measure time to place holds after incident declaration
Review gaps where data was lost to retention before a hold applied
Update the hold template with systems found missing

splunk.title: Export SIEM events for preservation
splunk.spl: index=* (host IN ("<host1>","<host2>") OR user="<custodian>") earliest=<hold_start> latest=<hold_end> | table _time index sourcetype host user _raw | outputcsv legal_hold_<case_id>.csv

splunk.title: Index retention that will drop relevant data
splunk.spl: | rest /services/data/indexes | table title frozenTimePeriodInSecs maxTotalDataSizeMB | eval retention_days=round(frozenTimePeriodInSecs/86400,0) | where retention_days < 365

splunk.title: Mailbox hold actions applied
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("New-CaseHoldPolicy","Set-CaseHoldPolicy","New-CaseHoldRule","Set-Mailbox") | search "LitigationHoldEnabled" OR Operation=*CaseHold* | table _time UserId Operation ObjectId

playbooks.name: Breach notice received from a third-party processor or vendor
playbooks.summary: Use when a vendor, SaaS provider or data processor notifies you that a breach on their side affected your data, and you must assess your exposure and your own notification duties as controller.

preparation: Keep a vendor register with data types shared, contract breach clauses and security contacts
Require processors to notify without undue delay in data processing agreements
Maintain integration and credential inventories per vendor
identification: Record when and how the vendor notified you, since your own clocks may start on receipt
Request from the vendor: timeline, data types, records affected, attacker access and indicators
Determine which of your data sets and customers the vendor held
Check whether vendor-held credentials, tokens or integrations into your environment were exposed
Search your logs for vendor indicators or abnormal activity from the vendor's integration
containment: Rotate API keys, OAuth tokens and service accounts used by the vendor integration
Restrict or pause the integration until the vendor confirms containment
Preserve the vendor's notice and all correspondence
eradication: Review vendor-provided indicators against your EDR and network logs
Remove excess data shared with the vendor beyond what the service needs
Obtain the vendor's remediation evidence or third-party forensic summary
recovery: Decide with Legal and Privacy whether you must notify regulators and individuals as controller
Coordinate notification content with the vendor to avoid conflicting messages
Re-enable the integration with new credentials and least-privilege scopes
lessons: Reassess the vendor's risk tier and contract terms
Measure delay between vendor incident and their notice to you
Review data minimization for all vendors in the same category

splunk.title: Activity from the vendor integration identity
splunk.spl: index=* (sourcetype="azure:aad:signin" appId="<vendor_app_id>") OR (sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" userIdentity.arn="*<vendor_role>*") earliest=<vendor_incident_start> | stats count values(ipAddress) as ips values(sourceIPAddress) as aws_ips by sourcetype

splunk.title: Vendor-provided indicators in network logs
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest IN ("<ioc_ip1>","<ioc_ip2>") OR All_Traffic.src IN ("<ioc_ip1>","<ioc_ip2>") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_port

splunk.title: OAuth token use by the vendor app
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" AppId="<vendor_app_id>" | stats count values(Operation) as ops earliest(_time) as first latest(_time) as last by ClientIP | convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

playbooks.name: Unlawful cross-border transfer of personal data discovered
playbooks.summary: Use when you find personal data being transferred or stored in a country without an adequate legal mechanism, such as a new SaaS region, offshore support or replicated backups.

preparation: Record approved transfer mechanisms such as SCCs, adequacy decisions or BCRs per vendor and region
Configure cloud policy to restrict resource creation to approved regions
Require transfer impact assessments before onboarding offshore processors
identification: Identify the data set, destination country and system or vendor involved
Determine how long the transfer has occurred and the volume of records
Check whether any transfer mechanism or impact assessment exists
Identify whether data residency laws in the source country prohibit the transfer outright
Establish who approved the configuration or vendor
containment: Pause replication or transfer to the non-approved region where operationally possible
Restrict access by offshore personnel to the data set pending review
Document the facts for the DPO and Legal
eradication: Move data back to an approved region or put SCCs and supplementary measures in place
Delete copies stored in the non-approved region once migration is verified
Apply region restriction policies to prevent recurrence
recovery: Update the record of processing and transfer register
Assess with counsel whether regulator engagement or disclosure is warranted
Confirm the service runs correctly in the approved region
lessons: Add region compliance checks to cloud deployment pipelines
Review procurement checks that missed the vendor's hosting location
Brief engineering teams on data residency requirements

splunk.title: Resources created in non-approved cloud regions
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="aws:cloudtrail" eventName IN ("CreateBucket","RunInstances","CreateDBInstance","PutBucketReplication") NOT awsRegion IN ("<approved_region1>","<approved_region2>") | stats count values(eventName) as events by awsRegion userIdentity.arn

splunk.title: Data flows to non-approved countries
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytes from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_category="pii_store" by All_Traffic.dest | iplocation All_Traffic.dest | lookup approved_countries.csv Country OUTPUT approved | where isnull(approved)

playbooks.name: Records retention failure: data kept too long or deleted too early
playbooks.summary: Use when records were retained past their schedule (expanding breach impact or violating law) or destroyed before their required retention period, including during a legal hold.

preparation: Maintain a records retention schedule mapping record types to systems and periods
Automate deletion jobs and log every purge with record counts
Make legal holds override automated deletion in each system
identification: Determine whether the failure is over-retention, premature deletion or deletion under hold
Identify the record types, systems, volumes and date ranges affected
Find the cause: disabled purge job, misconfigured policy, manual deletion or migration error
Check if deleted records were subject to a legal hold or regulatory retention rule
Assess whether over-retained data increased the impact of any related breach
containment: Stop the faulty deletion job or policy immediately if premature deletion is ongoing
Preserve remaining records and backups that might allow restoration
Notify Legal if records under hold were affected so counsel can address spoliation risk
eradication: Restore prematurely deleted records from backup where possible
Purge over-retained records under a documented and approved disposal run
Correct the retention policy configuration in the affected system
recovery: Verify purge and retention jobs run correctly on the next cycle
Record the disposal certificate or restoration evidence
Report to the regulator or court through counsel if required
lessons: Add monitoring for purge jobs that fail or delete unexpected volumes
Review migration runbooks for retention metadata handling
Reconcile the retention schedule against systems annually

splunk.title: Purge and retention job runs with counts
splunk.spl: index=* sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Operation IN ("ApplyRecordLabel","HardDelete","DispositionReviewAction","RetentionPolicyApplied") | timechart span=1d count by Operation

splunk.title: Mass deletions on records systems
splunk.spl: | tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Change where All_Changes.action=deleted All_Changes.dest IN ("<records_system>") by All_Changes.user _time span=1h | where count > 1000

splunk.title: Data older than retention in Splunk indexes
splunk.spl: | tstats min(_time) as oldest where index=* by index | eval age_days=round((now()-oldest)/86400,0) | lookup retention_schedule.csv index OUTPUT max_days | where age_days > max_days
